qs.q: A patient with chronic granulomatous disease presents with recurrent catalase-positive bacterial infections. Which specific defect in the phagocyte respiratory burst is most likely responsible for this clinical presentation?
o: Defective NADPH oxidase enzyme complex activity
Impaired phagolysosome fusion and degradation
Absent neutrophil chemotactic receptor signaling
Reduced production of pro-inflammatory cytokines
Failure of opsonization by complement components
qs.e: Chronic granulomatous disease is caused by defective NADPH oxidase, preventing the respiratory burst needed to kill catalase-positive organisms.

qs.q: A patient with chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) has a defect in the NADPH oxidase complex. Which specific component is often mutated in the X-linked form?
o: CYBB gene encoding the gp91^phox subunit
CYBA gene encoding the p22^phox subunit
NCF1 gene encoding the p47^phox subunit
NCF2 gene encoding the p67^phox subunit
RAC2 gene encoding the Rac2 GTPase
qs.e: X-linked CGD is caused by mutations in the CYBB gene, encoding the gp91phox subunit of NADPH oxidase.

qs.q: A patient with chronic granulomatous disease develops an invasive fungal infection characterized by septate hyphae branching at acute angles. Which neutrophil defect predisposes this patient to Aspergillus invasion?
o: Impaired degranulation of myeloperoxidase enzymes in cells
Defective phagolysosome acidification in circulating monocytes
Absence of surface complement receptors on circulating cells
Inability to generate reactive oxygen species via NADPH oxidase
Inadequate integrin expression required for vascular rolling
qs.e: NADPH oxidase deficiency prevents neutrophils from producing oxidative metabolites needed to kill engulfed hyphal fungal elements.

qs.q: In a patient with chronic granulomatous disease (CGD), neutrophils fail to kill ingested bacteria. Which enzyme complex is deficient?
o: NADPH oxidase complex in the phagosomal membrane
Myeloperoxidase within the primary azurophilic granules
Inducible nitric oxide synthase in the macrophage cytoplasm
Cyclooxygenase-2 localized to the endoplasmic reticulum
5-lipoxygenase associated with the nuclear membrane
qs.e: CGD results from inherited deficiencies in components of NADPH oxidase (phagocyte oxidase), which is essential for the respiratory burst that generates superoxide (O2•) and subsequent reactive oxygen species. This enzyme complex normally assembles rapidly when neutrophils phagocytose bacteria - cytosolic components translocate to the phagosomal membrane to form the active enzyme. exam: A 3‑year‑old presents with recurrent skin abscesses and a negative NBT test – what is the most likely diagnosis and why? — CGD; NBT negative indicates defective oxidative burst.
How would you differentiate CGD from severe combined immunodeficiency on laboratory testing? — CGD has normal lymphocyte counts and a defective DHR; SCID shows lymphopenia and absent T‑cell function.

A child with CGD develops a lung cavity on X‑ray; which organism is most likely and what is the first‑line treatment? — Aspergillus spp.; start voriconazole (or itraconazole if voriconazole unavailable).
Explain why prophylactic trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole is essential in CGD. — It covers common bacterial pathogens, especially Staph aureus and Serratia, reducing severe infections.
In a low‑resource setting without flow cytometry, how can you confirm CGD? — Perform the NBT test; a negative result strongly supports CGD.
What are the contraindicated drugs in CGD and why? — Live bacterial vaccines (e.g., BCG) and granulocyte‑colony stimulating factor without infection control can exacerbate granuloma formation.

A patient with CGD presents with abdominal pain and a mass; what complication should you suspect and how to investigate? — Granulomatous intestinal obstruction; obtain abdominal ultrasound or CT if available.
Discuss the curative option for CGD and its feasibility in East Africa. — Hematopoietic stem‑cell transplant can cure CGD but is limited by donor availability, cost, and infrastructure.
ai.title: Chronic Granulomatous Disease
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: CGD is an inherited defect of the NADPH‑oxidase complex causing impaired respiratory burst in phagocytes. Patients present with recurrent bacterial and fungal infections and granuloma formation, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: X‑linked CYBB mutation accounts for ~65% of cases.
Autosomal‑recessive forms (CYBA, NCF1, NCF2, NCF4) are more common in consanguineous populations.
sections.p: CGD is a primary immunodeficiency caused by X‑linked or autosomal‑recessive mutations in genes encoding the NADPH‑oxidase enzyme complex. The defect prevents generation of reactive oxygen species needed to kill certain catalase‑positive microbes.

b: Key organisms: Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia marcescens, Burkholderia cepacia, Nocardia spp., Aspergillus spp.
sections.p: The disease is not caused by a pathogen; rather, the host’s neutrophils and macrophages cannot produce superoxide. This predisposes to infections by catalase‑positive organisms that can neutralise residual hydrogen peroxide.

b: X‑linked: mothers are carriers; 50 % of male offspring affected.
Autosomal‑recessive: both parents carriers; 25 % risk per pregnancy.
sections.p: CGD is inherited, not transmitted infectiously. Genetic counseling is essential for families, especially where consanguinity is common.

b: In low‑resource settings, co‑infection with HIV or TB worsens outcomes.
sections.p: Patients develop recurrent skin, lymph node, lung, liver, and bone infections, often with abscesses that may become granulomatous. Granulomas can obstruct gastrointestinal or genitourinary tracts, mimicking Crohn’s disease or urinary obstruction.
Laboratory confirmation relies on functional tests of the oxidative burst and, where available, genetic testing.

t.b: Does the neutrophil reduce NBT to formazan? Positive (blue) = normal; Negative (no colour) = CGD.
Measures fluorescence after stimulation; Absent or markedly reduced fluorescence indicates CGD. Preferred when flow cytometer is available.

t.a: Genetic sequencing (targeted panel or whole exome)
t.b: Identifies specific mutation; guides prognosis and family counselling. If unavailable, rely on functional tests.
Identifies catalase‑positive pathogen; guides antimicrobial choice.

b: Acute infection: start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering Staph, Serratia, and Gram‑negatives; add antifungal (e.g., itraconazole) if fungal signs.
Prophylaxis: trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole daily to prevent bacterial infections; itraconazole or posaconazole weekly for fungal prophylaxis.
Interferon‑γ 1 µg/kg thrice weekly reduces severe infections; consider if injectable drugs are accessible.
Hematopoietic stem‑cell transplant (HSCT) is curative but often unavailable in low‑resource settings.
sections.p: Management combines infection control, prophylaxis, and immune modulation. In resource‑limited hospitals, emphasis is on readily available drugs and preventive measures.

t.b: Detects neutrophilia or anemia from chronic infection; normal counts do not exclude CGD.
Monitor inflammatory burden; very high ferritin may suggest uncontrolled infection.

b: CGD vs. SCID: CGD has normal lymphocyte numbers, defective neutrophil killing; SCID shows lymphopenia.
CGD vs. Hyper‑IgE (Job) syndrome: both have staph infections, but Job has eczema, high IgE, and skeletal abnormalities.
Absence of BCG scar in a vaccinated child with recurrent infections may hint at CGD in TB‑endemic areas.
sections.p: Key points examiners love: pathophysiology of the oxidative burst, typical organisms, diagnostic tests, prophylactic regimen, and differences from other primary immunodeficiencies.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly expanding soft‑tissue abscess, especially in the neck or mediastinum
Severe dyspnoea from pulmonary infiltrates or empyema
Signs of sepsis (hypotension, altered mental status) despite antibiotics
